title: P0: Bind per-FM MCP config transforms inside doctor mutate authority
description: The per-FM wrong-MCP-URL and stale-bearer-token fixers parse a pathname before entering mutate(), render replacement bytes from that snapshot, then mutate() hashes and backs up whatever inode is current later. Because mutate() has no expected-source precondition, its post-backup hash check cannot detect that the rendered replacement is stale. The fixers also do not keep one no-follow directory/file authority across read, Git exposure decision, backup, and publication; a parent swap can redirect writes out of scope, and the bearer-token fixer can write a literal credential to a Git-tracked config without the setup secret guard.
acceptance_criteria: Both per-FM MCP config repairs re-read and transform only after entering the canonical mutate chokepoint under a retained no-follow directory/file authority. The same source snapshot feeds semantic validation and a verbatim mode-safe doctor backup; any leaf, parent, inode, content, mode, or hardlink-topology change fails closed. Literal-secret Git tracked/ignored authority is serialized and remains valid through publication. Atomic replacement detaches hardlinks. Undo/action logs remain truthful and reversible. Mutation-red tests cover detector-to-fixer stale parse, parent and leaf swaps, tracked config refusal, outside hardlink to tracked file, backup source fidelity, dotted keys, ordinary URL/token repair, and no secret in logs. Targeted tests, workspace check, clippy with warnings denied, and fmt pass remotely.

comments.text:
# T3.6: Wire am bench CLI Subcommand

## What to build
Add a `Bench` variant to the CLI enum that orchestrates DB seeding, benchmark execution,
statistics computation, and baseline comparison.

## CLI interface
```
am bench [--quick] [--json] [--baseline <path>] [--save-baseline <path>]
         [--filter <pattern>] [--list] [--warmup N] [--runs N]
```

Flags:
- --quick: Fewer warmup (1) and runs (3) for faster feedback
- --json: Machine-readable JSON output (full BenchSummary)
- --baseline: Compare against a saved baseline file
- --save-baseline: Save current results as a new baseline
- --filter: Glob pattern to select specific benchmarks (e.g. "mail_*")
- --list: List available benchmarks without running them
- --warmup: Override warmup count (default 3)
- --runs: Override measurement count (default 10)

## Execution flow
1. Parse flags, determine benchmark set (filter or all)
2. Build release binary if needed (cargo build --release)
3. Create temp workspace for benchmark DB
4. Seed benchmark DB via seed_bench_db()
5. Set environment variables (MCP_AGENT_MAIL_DB, MCP_AGENT_MAIL_ARCHIVE_ROOT)
6. Run each benchmark via run_timed()
7. Compute stats via compute_stats()
8. If --baseline, compare via compare_baseline()
9. If --save-baseline, save via save_baseline()
10. Generate BenchSummary, write to benches/results/summary_<timestamp>.json
11. Print human-readable or JSON output

## Human-readable output example
```
[bench] Benchmarking with: target/release/am
[bench] Warmup: 3, Runs: 10

Benchmark               Mean      Stddev    P95       P99       vs Baseline
help                    2.31ms    0.12ms    2.45ms    2.52ms    -0.05ms (ok)
mail_inbox              14.23ms   0.89ms    15.67ms   16.12ms   +1.23ms (WARN)
mail_send               8.45ms    0.34ms    9.01ms    9.23ms    (no baseline)
```

CLIPBOARD AND EXPORT GUIDE (2026-02-13, RubyPrairie):

CLIPBOARD via OSC 52:
OSC 52 is a terminal escape sequence that copies text to the system clipboard.

HTML export is most useful because it preserves all colors and can be embedded in GitHub

SVG export is useful for presentations (scalable, crisp at any zoom level).

title: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed on all am commands due to SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS
description:
FIXED: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed on every am command.

Root cause: The statically linked SQLite (libsqlite3.a) is compiled with SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS, which enables PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON by default for every new connection. Our code never explicitly set foreign_keys = OFF, so every INSERT/UPDATE on tables with REFERENCES clauses was subject to FK enforcement. Any orphan data (e.g. agents referencing deleted projects) caused cascading "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" errors.

Fix: Added PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF as the FIRST pragma in all 5 connection initialization paths:
1. PRAGMA_SETTINGS_SQL (CLI sync connections)
2. PRAGMA_DB_INIT_SQL (pool WAL init)
3. PRAGMA_DB_INIT_BASE_SQL (pool base mode init)
4. PRAGMA_CONN_SETTINGS_SQL (static per-conn settings)
5. build_conn_pragmas() (dynamic per-conn settings with budget-aware cache)

The REFERENCES clauses in CREATE TABLE DDL are kept for documentation but have no runtime effect with foreign_keys = OFF.

Discovery: Confirmed via strings /data/tmp/cargo-target/release/am | grep DEFAULT_FOREIGN → DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS. The system sqlite3 tool does NOT have this flag (PRAGMA compile_options does not list it), but the statically linked libsqlite3.a does. Since ldd shows no dynamic libsqlite3.so, the binary uses the static lib.

Verification: All 517 DB tests + 583 CLI tests pass. Manual smoke test of agents list, agents register, doctor check all succeed.
close_reason: done

title: ATC1: atc_experiences hard-cap rotation + lower default + vacuum (open-row backlog can't bloat DB/startup)
description: REAL INCIDENT (css, 2026-06-15): storage.sqlite3 grew to 2.6GB, 2.41GB of it one table atc_experiences (629,033 rows in 6 days); rollups empty; startup replayed the whole ledger (104GB reads, 10GB RSS, port never bound). ROOT CAUSE: enforce_experience_row_ceiling evicts ONLY terminal (resolved/censored/expired) rows; when the backlog is OPEN/unresolved it logs 'no terminal rows evictable' and leaves the table unchanged -> unbounded. Also default ceiling atc_experience_max_rows=250_000 is far too high (~1-2.5GB of fat JSON rows), DELETE doesn't reclaim space without VACUUM, and v0.3.12 predates the ceiling entirely. FIX: (1) make the ceiling a true hard cap - when terminal eviction is insufficient, rotate oldest rows by experience_id regardless of state down to target (boundedness > preserving stale open rows); (2) lower default ceiling to a sane bound; (3) VACUUM/incremental reclaim after eviction; (4) reduce write spam if no-op decisions persist rows; (5) bound startup ledger load. ACCEPTANCE: table provably bounded by max_rows even with 100% open rows; unit test for open-backlog rotation; default keeps table small.
close_reason: Fixed + committed b80d1a0a. enforce_experience_row_ceiling is now a true hard cap: terminal-first eviction (rollups preserved), then force-rotate oldest rows regardless of state when an open backlog exceeds the cap -> table provably bounded. Default ceiling 250k->50k, sweep 1h->15min. 2 new tests + existing ceiling tests pass via rch; clippy core+db clean. Addresses the css 2.41GB/629k-row atc_experiences bloat that wedged startup. Daily VACUUM reclaims freed pages.

title: ATC Track 13: Mechanism Design — Incentive-Compatible Conflict Resolution
description:
# Track 13: Mechanism Design for Fair Conflict Resolution

## Alien-Artifact Source: §29 Game Theory + Mechanism Design
## Key math: VCG mechanism, Shapley value, Price of Anarchy

## The Insight That Changes Everything
The current ATC is a DICTATOR — it decides who releases reservations in a
deadlock based on its own scoring function. This creates resentment: agents
that repeatedly get told to yield will learn to game the system (reserve
aggressively, refuse to release, ignore advisories).

The mechanism design insight: instead of dictating outcomes, DESIGN RULES
so that agents acting in their own self-interest naturally produce globally
optimal outcomes. Make truthful cooperation the dominant strategy.

## Why This Matters for Users
With the current design:
- Agent A always loses conflicts because it registered later → unfair
- Agents learn to "frontrun" reservations to game the scoring → wasteful
- The ATC's scoring weights are arbitrary → hard to justify to operators

With mechanism design:
- Priority is determined by DECLARED remaining work (truthful reporting
  is provably optimal — lying hurts you)
- No agent is systematically disadvantaged
- The mechanism has a mathematical fairness guarantee (Shapley axioms)
- The operator doesn't need to tune scoring weights — the mechanism is
  self-balancing

## Core Mechanism: Priority Auction for Contested Resources

### How It Works
When a deadlock is detected (or a hard conflict arises), instead of the ATC
unilaterally picking a loser, it runs a priority auction:

1. ATC sends a structured "priority declaration" request to each agent
   in the cycle:
   ```
   [ATC] Conflict on {patterns}. Please reply with your priority
   declaration (see thread for format).
   ```

2. Each agent replies with:
   ```json
   { "remaining_tasks": 5, "estimated_completion_mins": 30,
     "willing_to_yield": true, "yield_cost_estimate": "low" }
   ```

3. The ATC computes priority using a VCG-inspired rule:

```rust
/// VCG-inspired priority: each agent's priority is determined by
/// the EXTERNALITY they impose on others by holding the resource.
///
/// Priority = sum of OTHER agents' declared costs if this agent
/// keeps the resource. The agent with the HIGHEST externality
/// (most blocking impact on others) yields first.
fn vcg_priority(
    agents: &[ConflictParticipant],
    contested_patterns: &[String],
) -> Vec<(AgentId, f64)> {
    let mut priorities = Vec::new();
    for (i, agent) in agents.iter().enumerate() {
        // Externality: how much does THIS agent holding the resource
        // cost everyone else?
        let externality: f64 = agents.iter()
            .enumerate()
            .filter(|(j, _)| *j != i)
            .map(|(_, other)| {
                other.remaining_tasks as f64
                    * other.estimated_completion_mins as f64
                    / 60.0 // cost in agent-hours
            })
            .sum();
        priorities.push((agent.id.clone(), externality));
    }
    // Highest externality = should yield first (they're blocking the most)
    priorities.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.partial_cmp(&a.1).unwrap_or(std::cmp::Ordering::Equal));
    priorities
}
```

### Why Truthful Reporting Is Optimal
Under the VCG mechanism, lying about your remaining work HURTS you:
- If you UNDERREPORT (say 1 task when you have 10): your externality
  appears low → you DON'T yield → but you actually needed more time,
  so you finish late and others were blocked for nothing
- If you OVERREPORT (say 50 tasks when you have 2): your externality
  appears high → you yield → you lose the resource even though you
  were almost done

Truthful reporting minimizes your expected cost. This is provable (VCG
incentive compatibility theorem).

### Fallback: Non-Responsive Agents
If an agent doesn't respond within 30 seconds:
- Assume worst-case: remaining_tasks = 0, willing_to_yield = true
- This incentivizes responsiveness (non-response = automatic yield)
- Logged as "default priority declaration" in evidence ledger

### Shapley-Based Cost Sharing
When a deadlock resolution costs an agent time (they had to redo work after
yielding their reservation), the ATC tracks the cost and uses Shapley values
to compute fair attribution:

```rust
/// Compute each agent's Shapley value for the cost of this conflict.
/// Agents who caused more of the conflict (by holding more contested
/// patterns) bear more of the cost attribution.
fn shapley_cost_attribution(
    conflict: &ResolvedConflict,
    agents: &[AgentId],
) -> HashMap<AgentId, f64> {
    // Shapley value: average marginal contribution across all orderings
    // For 2-3 agents this is exact; for more, use sampling
}
```

This cost attribution is surfaced in the session summary (Track 7) and
helps operators understand WHICH agents are causing disproportionate conflict.

## Price of Anarchy Monitoring
The ATC continuously monitors the efficiency loss from selfish agent behavior:

```
PoA = actual_total_wait_time / optimal_total_wait_time
```

If PoA exceeds 1.5 (50% efficiency loss from selfishness), the ATC escalates
to the operator: "Agent coordination efficiency has degraded. Consider
restructuring task assignments."

## Dependency
- Requires Track 3 (Conflict Detector) — provides deadlock cycles to resolve
- Requires Track 4 (Evidence Ledger) — logs priority declarations and outcomes
- Enhances Track 3's deadlock resolution protocol with game-theoretic fairness
- Track 8 (Integration) wires this module into the conflict resolution path
  at the engine level (Track 13 is a standalone algorithm, Track 8 orchestrates)

## Files
- crates/mcp-agent-mail-server/src/atc.rs (mechanism module within ATC)

## Tests
- Unit: VCG priority correctly identifies highest-externality agent
- Unit: truthful reporting produces lower cost than any deviation
- Unit: non-responsive agent gets default (yield) priority
- Unit: Shapley attribution sums to total conflict cost
- Unit: PoA monitoring detects efficiency degradation
- Property: VCG priority is incentive-compatible (no profitable deviation)
- Property: Shapley values satisfy efficiency + symmetry + null player axioms
- Integration: full auction cycle (request → declare → resolve → attribute)

## SECOND-PASS CORRECTION: Track 5 Real Gaps

### T5.2 — .env File Search is a REAL GAP
The Rust config.rs loads .env from the CURRENT WORKING DIRECTORY only.
The bash scripts/am searches these specific paths:
  1. ~/.mcp_agent_mail/.env (preferred)
  2. ~/mcp_agent_mail/.env (legacy, no dot prefix)

This is a REAL gap — when agents run from their project directory (e.g., /data/projects/foo),
the CWD .env won't have the Agent Mail token. The bash wrapper handles this by
explicitly searching the home-directory-based paths.

T5.2 should add the home-directory .env search to Config::from_env() or
to the serve command startup, using the same precedence as bash:
  1. Environment variable (already works)
  2. ~/.mcp_agent_mail/.env
  3. ~/mcp_agent_mail/.env
  4. CWD .env (already works)

### T5.1 — Port Detection Limitations
The bash uses lsof to get the PID of the listener. TcpListener::bind() only tells
you if the port is available, NOT what process holds it.

For full parity, Rust needs to either:
a) Shell out to `lsof -tiTCP:{port} -sTCP:LISTEN` (platform-specific but matches bash)
b) Read /proc/net/tcp on Linux (more robust, no external dep)
c) Just try to bind and report the error (simpler but loses PID info)

Option (a) is recommended for parity. The PID is needed to check if the
existing process is mcp_agent_mail / mcp-agent-mail (vs a foreign process).

### T5.4 — --env-file flag
The bash supports --env-file <path> to override the default .env search.
Check if the Rust main.rs already has this flag. If not, add it.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Track 1: am ci — Native Local CI Gate Runner

## What it replaces
scripts/ci.sh (287 lines of bash)

## Current behavior
The bash script runs 13 quality/performance/security/docs gates sequentially:
- cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy, cargo build, cargo test
- mode_matrix_harness, semantic_conformance, perf_security_regressions, help_snapshots
- Release docs presence check
- E2E suites (dual-mode, mode matrix, security/privacy, TUI accessibility)

It tracks pass/fail/skip per gate, times each gate with `date +%s` (1-second granularity),
and generates a structured JSON gate report using a 100-line jq pipeline. Supports
--quick (skip E2E) and --report <path> flags.

## External dependencies eliminated
- **jq**: The entire JSON gate report (lines 103-276) depends on jq. Rust's serde_json
  handles this natively with proper typing.

## Key improvements
1. **Parallel gate execution**: Bash runs all gates sequentially. Independent gates
   (fmt + clippy + docs check) can run simultaneously, cutting total CI time by 30-40%.
2. **Sub-millisecond timing**: date +%s gives 1-second granularity. Rust Instant gives
   nanosecond precision — critical for benchmarking fast gates.
3. **Structured error capture**: When a gate fails, bash just says "FAIL". Rust can
   capture stderr, parse compiler/test output, and produce actionable failure details.
4. **Cross-platform**: No bash-specific constructs, works on Windows with cargo.
5. **Typed gate report**: The JSON report schema (am_ci_gate_report.v1) becomes a proper
   Rust struct with serde, eliminating the 100-line jq pipeline.

## CLI interface
```
am ci [--quick] [--report <path>] [--parallel] [--json]
```

## Implementation location
crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/ci.rs (new module)
Wire into Cli enum in crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/lib.rs

## Files to read for context
- scripts/ci.sh (the script being replaced)
- crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/lib.rs (CLI structure to extend)
- tests/artifacts/ci/gate_report.json (example output format)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# T3.5: Implement Baseline Management

## What to build
Save, load, and compare benchmark baselines for regression detection. Replaces
the BENCH_BASELINE_FILE logic in the Python aggregation script.

## Key behaviors
1. **Save baseline**: Write current benchmark results to a JSON file (--save-baseline)
2. **Load baseline**: Read a previously saved baseline file
3. **Compare**: For each benchmark, compute delta_p95_ms = current.p95 - baseline.p95
4. **Regression detection**: Flag if delta_p95_ms > threshold (default: 10% of baseline)

## Rust implementation
```rust
/// Baseline file format: map of benchmark name → p95_ms value
type BaselineData = BTreeMap<String, f64>;

fn save_baseline(results: &BTreeMap<String, BenchResult>, path: &Path) -> Result<(), Error>

fn load_baseline(path: &Path) -> Result<BaselineData, Error>

fn compare_baseline(
    results: &BTreeMap<String, BenchResult>,
    baseline: &BaselineData,
    threshold_pct: f64,   // e.g. 0.10 for 10%
) -> Vec<BaselineComparison>

struct BaselineComparison {
    name: String,
    current_p95_ms: f64,
    baseline_p95_ms: f64,
    delta_p95_ms: f64,
    delta_pct: f64,
    regression: bool,
}
```

## Implementation notes
- Baseline file is simple JSON: `{"help": 2.5, "mail_inbox": 15.3, ...}`
- This matches the format expected by the Python script (BENCH_BASELINE_FILE)
- Benchmarks not present in the baseline get baseline_p95_ms=null, regression=false
- Regression threshold is configurable but defaults to 10%
- Print regression warnings in human-readable output (highlighted in red if terminal)

## Location
crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/bench.rs (baseline functions)

title: [completion-debt of br-8ujfs.6.7] F8 archive boot-time integrity check — preflight_archive_integrity, BootCheckMode, BootCheckReport, env vars, startup wiring, TUI panel, tests
description:
# F8: Archive boot-time integrity check + self-repair

## Why this debt exists

Original `br-8ujfs.6.7` was closed in pass 2 with the closer (1502) admitting the entire deliverable was deferred ('architectural'). Verification: zero references in the codebase to `preflight_archive_integrity`, `BootCheckMode`, `BootCheckReport`, `AM_BOOT_CHECK_MODE`, or `AM_BOOT_AUTO_REPAIR`. No startup wiring, no TUI panel, no integration or e2e tests.

## Spec — preserves all original requirements verbatim

The mcp-agent-mail archive (per-project Git repos under `STORAGE_ROOT`) is itself a git repo. If 2.51.0 damaged the archive BEFORE the fix shipped, the server might fail to start — or worse, start with corrupt archive and silently overwrite good data. F1-F6 give ops a tool for USER repos. F8 ensures the ARCHIVE is healthy at boot so we don't compound damage.

## Current state

- Boot path: server entry in `crates/mcp-agent-mail/src/main.rs` calls into `crates/mcp-agent-mail-server/src/lib.rs::serve_http` / `serve_stdio`.
- Recovery code: `crates/mcp-agent-mail-storage/src/recovery.rs` exists with detection helpers.
- F2 detect-orphan-refs (libgit2-native) likely lives in `recovery.rs` or `crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/doctor_orphan_refs.rs`.
- F3 prune + F4 repack: also in those modules; gated behind explicit operator invocation.
- TUI System Health screen: `tui_screens/system_health.rs` (4049 lines) — has badge infrastructure ready.
- No pre-boot validation hook today.

## Target state — `preflight_archive_integrity` + boot wiring

### Deliverable A — Module + types in `crates/mcp-agent-mail-storage/src/boot_check.rs` (new file)

```rust
pub enum BootCheckMode { Warn, Abort, AutoRepair }

#[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize)]
pub struct BootCheckFinding {
    pub project: String,
    pub kind: BootCheckFindingKind,
    pub detail: String,
}

#[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize)]
pub enum BootCheckFindingKind {
    RepoBroken,           // git2::Repository::open failed
    OrphanRefs(Vec<String>), // F2 missing-refs result
    DanglingBranch(String),  // commit-tree without ref
    ConfigCorrupt(String),   // .git/config malformed
    AutoRepaired { actions: Vec<String> }, // when AutoRepair mode + repair succeeded
}

#[derive(Debug, serde::Serialize)]
pub struct BootCheckReport {
    pub mode: BootCheckMode,
    pub root: PathBuf,
    pub started_at: String,         // RFC3339
    pub completed_at: String,
    pub duration_ms: u64,
    pub total_projects: u32,
    pub findings: Vec<BootCheckFinding>,
    pub auto_repaired_count: u32,
}

pub fn preflight_archive_integrity(root: &Path, mode: BootCheckMode) -> BootCheckReport;
```

Implementation steps (verbatim from original):
1. For each project under `STORAGE_ROOT/<slug>/`:
   - try `git2::Repository::open` — if fails: `RepoBroken { project, error }`
2. For each open-able repo:
   - run `detect_missing_refs` (libgit2-native, NEVER shell git)
   - if any missing: `OrphanRefs { project, refs }`
3. Return summary report.

### Deliverable B — Modes (verbatim from original)

- `Warn` (default): log findings, proceed with startup. `INFO boot_check_completed` event with full report.
- `Abort`: return `Err(BootCheckError::FindingsBlockBoot)`; main returns non-zero exit; server refuses to start.
- `AutoRepair`: call F3 (prune) + F4 (repack) for each finding. **Backups always written first** (per F3/F4 v3 backup convention). Audit record to evidence ledger.
  - **DANGER gate**: only enabled via explicit env `AM_BOOT_AUTO_REPAIR=I_UNDERSTAND_THE_RISKS`. The literal string. No abbreviations. If env is set to anything else (incl. `1` or `true`), AutoRepair refuses to run AND logs ERROR.

### Deliverable C — Default mode

- `AM_BOOT_CHECK_MODE=warn` (default): log + proceed.
- `AM_BOOT_CHECK_MODE=abort`: fail fast.
- `AM_BOOT_CHECK_MODE=auto_repair`: only effective when `AM_BOOT_AUTO_REPAIR=I_UNDERSTAND_THE_RISKS` is also set. Otherwise demoted to `warn` with ERROR log explaining the mismatch.

### Deliverable D — Startup logging (per E6 spec, cross-references br-j1qwr)

All events under tracing target `mcp_agent_mail::boot_check` with names:

- `boot_check_started` (INFO) — `{ root, mode, total_projects }`
- `boot_check_finding` (WARN per issue) — `{ project, kind, detail }`
- `boot_check_completed` (INFO) — `{ mode, total_projects, findings_count, auto_repaired_count, duration_ms }`
- `boot_check_aborted` (ERROR) — only when mode=abort and findings ≥ 1; followed by process exit
- `boot_check_auto_repair_attempted` (WARN) — per project in AutoRepair mode, `{ project, actions, before_state, after_state }`
- `boot_check_auto_repair_failed` (ERROR) — per project where repair errored
- `boot_check_auto_repair_gate_violated` (ERROR) — when `AM_BOOT_CHECK_MODE=auto_repair` set without `AM_BOOT_AUTO_REPAIR=I_UNDERSTAND_THE_RISKS`

JSON Schemas committed under `docs/schemas/git_251/boot_check.schema.json` (per br-j1qwr §4).

### Deliverable E — TUI surfacing

- System Health screen shows a `last boot check` panel: `{ ran_at, mode, total_projects, findings_count, auto_repaired_count }`.
- If findings exist AND mode=warn, persistent BADGE: `archive has N orphan refs across M projects. Run: am doctor fix-orphan-refs --all --dry-run`.
- Banner format and badge wiring follow F5 conventions (cross-references br-66evl).

### Deliverable F — Safety (verbatim)

- NEVER auto-repair unless explicit env override is set with the literal string.
- AutoRepair always writes backups (per F3/F4 v3 backup convention) BEFORE any mutation.
- AutoRepair writes an audit record to evidence ledger with full detail of changes.

## Performance budget

- `preflight_archive_integrity` p95 ≤ 100ms × N projects on healthy archive (libgit2-native, no shell forks).
- Worst-case timeout: 30s for entire archive sweep. Beyond: log WARN, demote to `abort` for safety, exit non-zero.

## Non-goals

- No archive auto-repair without the explicit env opt-in.
- Not changing F1-F6 user-facing tooling.
- Not invoking F3/F4 in `Warn` mode (detection only).

title: P1: Bind manual container tags to the full source dependency closure
description: The manual Docker source lane now resolves AM_REF to an immutable main-repository commit, but it still builds the path-patched frankensearch and beads_rust dependencies from mutable SIBLING_REF/SIBLING_FALLBACK_REF values (default main). Re-running the same source-sha-AM_COMMIT tag after either sibling advances can overwrite it with different binary bytes while preserving the same revision label.
acceptance_criteria: Resolve every path dependency used by Dockerfile to an immutable repository-specific 40-hex commit before build, reject ambiguous/short/moving post-resolution inputs, verify each Docker checkout HEAD equals its expected commit, and bind a deterministic closure identity into labels/provenance and non-overwriting manual tags. Mutation-sensitive tests prove moving either sibling cannot reproduce or overwrite the old identity. One real manual source build is inspected by digest and provenance before closure.

comments.text: Fresh-eyes Dockerfile trace also corrected the stale top-level claim that nine former sibling repositories are cloned. Current Cargo.toml/Dockerfile authority is exactly frankensearch plus beads_rust; source comment bytes now match the enforced clone-list guard. Full immutable closure binding remains open.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Fresh-eyes continuation: the identity gap also includes the build recipe. The build job checks out Dockerfile/workflow bytes from the triggering github.sha, while source tags and OCI revision currently name only the selected AM_REF. Re-running source-sha-<AM_REF> after main changes can therefore overwrite the tag with different Dockerfile/toolchain/workflow bytes even if both sibling commits are frozen. Closure must bind the exact builder/workflow revision (and pinned toolchain/lock inputs) alongside AM_REF and sibling commits in the non-overwriting identity and provenance.

title: Archive batch write performance: 100-message batch 4x over budget
description:
# Epic: Archive Batch Write Performance Regression

## Background

`benches/BUDGETS.md` (as of 2026-02-08 baselines, referenced in README L1295) records an acknowledged performance gap:

| Operation | Baseline p50 | Baseline p95 | Budget p95 | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single message, no attachments | ~17.2ms | ~21.3ms | < 25ms | Healthy |
| Single message, inline attachment | ~22.0ms | ~26.0ms | < 25ms | **1.04x over budget** (marginal) |
| Single message, file attachment | ~20.4ms | ~25.2ms | < 25ms | **1.01x over budget** (marginal) |
| Batch 100 messages | ~930ms | ~1076ms | < 250ms | **~4.3x over budget** |

README is honest about this ("The batch-write path is still above budget...") and the performance-epic beads (br-15dv) were closed in 2026-02-08, but this specific regression was never brought under budget. It has been stable for 2+ months.

## Why this matters

Multi-agent workloads routinely generate batched writes: macro_start_session bundles register + reserve + inbox-fetch; a session cleanup releases many reservations at once; a migration import ingests N messages in one transaction. A 4x budget overrun on batch writes translates directly to observable UI lag and commit-coalescer backpressure.

The single-message budgets are effectively met; this is purely the batch path.

## Hypotheses for root cause (to be validated, not assumed)

1. **Commit coalescer not actually batching** — if `coalesce.rs` is committing per-message despite receiving N enqueues in a window, we pay N git overhead instead of 1. The README claims "9.1x batching ratio (100 writes → 11 commits)" which suggests batching IS happening; but 100/11 ≈ 9x still means 11 commits for what could be 1 if we're patient.
2. **fsync strategy** — if WAL checkpoint or fsync is forced per message, we're paying disk-durability cost per row.
3. **Archive file layout** — if each message creates its own file AND its own directory entry (per-agent inbox copy + per-agent outbox copy + canonical), file-system overhead is multiplied.
4. **Per-message index update** — if the SQLite transaction or the ReadCache write-behind queue is doing per-message work that could be bulked, that's pure amortization gain.
5. **Hash/signature computation** — if commit coalescer hashes/signs each artifact independently, batch merging can deduplicate.
6. **Lock thrash** — `.archive.lock` taken N times instead of once per batch.

## Plan

Drill-down progression — each child task is a discrete investigation or fix:
- **Profile the batch path** with flamegraph + tracing span deltas, capture a golden profile artifact.
- **Identify dominant cost** (one of the hypotheses above, possibly more than one).
- **Implement targeted fix** (could be batching threshold tune, could be coalescer rework, could be archive layout change).
- **Benchmark under budget** — batch 100 messages p95 < 250ms on the same hardware BUDGETS.md baseline used.
- **Stress-test regression guard** — confirm no regression on single-message path or on 30-agent stress test.
- **Update BUDGETS.md** with new numbers and dated baseline.

## Non-goals (explicit)

- Not rewriting the storage layer. Targeted intervention only.
- Not changing the git-backed-archive design (artifact durability guarantee must be preserved).
- Not loosening the budget to match reality — that would be solving the wrong problem.
- Not optimizing single-message path (already within budget).

## Acceptance criteria

- Batch 100 messages p95 < 250ms on reference hardware
- Single-message p95 still < 25ms (no regression)
- Single-message with attachment p95 ≤ 25ms (fix the marginal 1.04x overrun as a side-effect if cheap)
- Stress tests still pass (30-agent, pool exhaustion, WBQ saturation, etc.)
- BUDGETS.md has a new dated row showing under-budget numbers
- reality-check re-run no longer flags archive batch writes as a gap
close_reason: Epic complete: all children shipped per IvorySummit review

# Archive perf task 1: Profile the batch path

## Scope

Before fixing anything, capture a precise profile of the `batch 100 messages` archive write path. The BUDGETS.md entry says 1076ms p95 vs 250ms budget — 4.3x over. The profile is the decisive input for where the fix goes.

## Setup

1. Identify the benchmark: `cargo bench -p mcp-agent-mail --bench benchmarks -- archive_write` exercises the batch path per README L1307.
2. Isolate the batch-100 case from the single-message cases.
3. Run with `cargo flamegraph` OR with `perf record` + `inferno-flamegraph`, capture 30-second sample.
4. Also capture structured tracing spans via `RUST_LOG=trace mcp_agent_mail_storage::archive=trace,mcp_agent_mail_storage::coalesce=trace` and parse span durations.
5. Capture comparison: batch-1 p95, batch-10 p95, batch-100 p95 — verify scaling law (linear? superlinear? shows coalescer breakdown?).

## Deliverables

- `tests/artifacts/perf/archive_batch_100_flamegraph.svg` (committed or linked)
- `tests/artifacts/perf/archive_batch_100_spans.json` (trace data)
- Top-10 span categories by cumulative duration, written as bulleted analysis in the profile report
- Scaling-law observation (e.g., "batch-100 takes 100x batch-1 → zero amortization" or "batch-100 takes 20x batch-1 → some amortization, but room for more")

## Considerations

- Run on the same hardware class as BUDGETS.md baselines (documented at the top of BUDGETS.md or infer from file)
- Ensure WAL mode + PRAGMA settings match production defaults
- Use a warm DB (not a cold new file) to avoid init-cost skew
- If Git operations dominate, capture which Git operations (object writing? packing? ref update?)
- If SQLite inserts dominate, capture per-query time
- If commit coalescer dominates, note the batching ratio actually observed

## Definition of done

- Profile artifacts committed
- Written analysis identifies dominant cost category (Git? SQLite? coalescer? fsync? file-layout?)
- Scaling-law measurement included

title: Archive perf 10: cross-filesystem fsync behavior — ext4, btrfs, xfs, APFS verification
description:
# Archive perf 10: Cross-filesystem fsync testing

## Why this bead exists

fsync() behavior varies dramatically across filesystems:
- **ext4**: fsync is reasonably fast with default data=ordered mode (~ms)
- **btrfs**: fsync involves CoW + metadata; can be slow (~10ms+)
- **xfs**: fsync is typically fast (~ms)
- **APFS (macOS)**: fsync is a barrier, not a flush — different durability semantics

The archive perf fix may be optimized for one FS and regress on another. MEMORY notes Linux ext4+xfs are most common for dev machines, but users on btrfs (increasingly common on Ubuntu, NixOS, Fedora Workstation) and macOS APFS need coverage.

## Scope

Add a cross-FS test matrix to CI and document known quirks.

### Test matrix

| Filesystem | Platform | In CI? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| ext4 (data=ordered) | Linux | Yes (default) | Most common; baseline |
| ext4 (data=journal) | Linux | Yes (separate runner) | Higher durability, slower |
| xfs | Linux | Yes (separate runner) | Fast fsync; common on servers |
| btrfs | Linux | Yes (separate runner) | Slow fsync; slow-batch concern |
| ZFS (on Linux) | Linux | No (skip; niche) | Documented as unsupported initially |
| APFS | macOS | Yes (mac runner) | Different durability semantics |
| NTFS (via WSL) | Windows | Yes (Windows runner via install.ps1 flow) | Low priority but native path |
| tmpfs | Any | Yes (negative test) | Should be FAST but not durable — document |

### Per-FS expectations

- ext4: p95 batch-100 < 250ms (the standard budget)
- btrfs: p95 batch-100 < 500ms acknowledged as a platform quirk; documented in BUDGETS.md per-FS
- xfs: p95 batch-100 < 250ms
- APFS: p95 batch-100 < 300ms; fsync is barrier-only, so semantics differ
- tmpfs: p95 batch-100 < 50ms (no disk I/O); runs as a drift-detection canary (if it regresses, it's pure compute/logic overhead)

### Documentation

Update `benches/BUDGETS.md` with per-FS rows. Update `docs/OPERATOR_RUNBOOK.md` with a "Filesystem guidance" section recommending ext4/xfs for best latency and acknowledging btrfs as supported-but-slower.

## Test plan

### Unit tests (per-FS parameterized)

For each FS in the matrix:
1. Single message write p95 under budget for that FS
2. Batch 100 write p95 under per-FS budget
3. `am doctor check` reports expected filesystem

### Integration

- Provision FS-specific CI runners OR use loopback mount of a fresh FS per test
- Bench runs per FS produce labeled baselines

### Verification

- Manual spot-check: run bench on a real btrfs laptop, verify numbers match CI-reported btrfs numbers within 10%
- Manual spot-check: same on macOS APFS

## Logging requirements

```
perf.filesystem.detected { fs_type, mount_options }
perf.filesystem.fsync_mode { mode: "normal"|"barrier_only"|"buffered" }
perf.filesystem.bench_start { operation, fs_type }
perf.filesystem.bench_complete { operation, fs_type, p50, p95, p99, vs_budget }
```

## Non-goals

- Not supporting every exotic FS
- Not rewriting the archive to abstract over FS semantics
- Not requiring each user to pick a specific FS (we document recommendations; they choose)

## Dependencies

- Depends on br-8qdh0.3 (fix implementation) — cross-FS matters only after the fix
- Depends on br-8qdh0.4 (bench verification) — verification in scope is ext4; this bead extends to other FSes

## Definition of done

- Cross-FS bench runners configured in CI (at least ext4 default + btrfs)
- Per-FS budget table in BUDGETS.md
- Filesystem guidance in runbook
- Tests pass on reference FSes
- Known-quirk notes documented (e.g., btrfs CoW amplification for archive writes)

title: Archive perf 11: extend perf suite with memory allocation + startup + p99.9 tail regression guard
description:
# Archive perf 11: Extended perf dimensions

## Why this bead exists

The main archive-perf epic focuses on p95 throughput. Three other dimensions could regress without catching:

1. **Memory allocation rate** — a fix that achieves faster p95 by allocating heap on every message instead of per-batch will work fine in benches but degrade under sustained load (GC pressure, allocator contention)
2. **Startup time** — if the fix changes an init path (e.g., pre-warming the coalescer with a larger buffer), startup latency might regress; `am serve-http` goes from < 500ms to several seconds
3. **p99.9 tail latency** — the fix might move the p95 under budget while introducing pathological p99.9 outliers (stop-the-world fsync batches, lock-contention stalls); rare but user-visible

Absent explicit guards, any of these three can ship as an unacknowledged regression.

## Scope

### Memory allocation regression

- Use `jemalloc`-stats or `tikv-jemalloc-ctl` to sample allocator state at bench start and end
- Assert: allocations per message < N (where N is the pre-fix baseline × 1.1)
- RSS growth over 1-hour soak < 100MB
- Integrated into criterion bench harness via custom instrumentation

### Startup time regression

- Extend `am bench` catalog with `cli_startup_serve_http` operation:
  - Measures time from `am serve-http` invocation to "listening on port" log line
  - Baseline: < 500ms
  - Budget: < 750ms (1.5× baseline)
- Similar for `am serve-stdio`, `am robot status --help`

### p99.9 tail latency

- Extend archive write benchmarks to capture full latency distribution, not just p50/p95/p99
- Report p99.9 (1-in-1000) and p99.99 (1-in-10000) alongside standard percentiles
- Budget: p99.9 < 5× budget-p95 (tail compression discipline)
- If p99.9 regresses > 50% vs baseline even when p95 is good: fail the bench + flag for investigation

### Cross-dimensional regression report

`tests/artifacts/perf/extended_dimensions_<date>.json` captures:
```json
{
  "memory": { "allocations_per_msg", "rss_growth_1h_mb", "allocator_stats" },
  "startup": { "serve_http_ms", "serve_stdio_ms", "cli_startup_ms" },
  "tail": { "p99_9_ms", "p99_99_ms", "worst_observed_ms", "tail_ratio" },
  "verdict": { "all_dimensions_pass", "regressions" }
}
```

## Test plan

### Unit

1. Memory test: 10K message inserts; measure allocator delta; assert under budget
2. Startup test: spawn + kill am serve-http 20 times; measure "listening" lag; p95 < budget
3. Tail test: 100K message inserts in criterion; extract full distribution; assert p99.9 under budget
4. Soak: 1-hour run; measure RSS growth; assert bounded

### Integration

- CI perf-gate (br-8qdh0.7) extended to include these three dimensions
- PR comment includes extended metrics alongside standard p50/p95

### Negative tests

- Deliberate leak: introduce a ref-cycle in test, verify soak detects RSS growth
- Deliberate tail regression: add a 1-in-1000 artificial stall, verify tail test catches it

## Logging requirements

```
perf.extended.memory_snapshot { phase: "start"|"end", rss_kb, allocations_total, bytes_allocated }
perf.extended.startup_sample { cli: "serve_http"|"serve_stdio"|"cli", ms }
perf.extended.tail_distribution { operation, p50, p75, p90, p95, p99, p99_9, p99_99, max }
perf.extended.regression_detected { dimension, baseline, current, delta_pct }
```

## Non-goals

- Not an allocator study (one metric, one threshold, not a deep investigation)
- Not guaranteeing zero tail latency (that's impossible under real workloads)
- Not measuring GC pauses in non-Rust contexts (Rust doesn't have GC)

## Dependencies

- Depends on br-8qdh0.3 (fix implementation) — measurements are meaningful only post-fix
- Depends on br-8qdh0.4 (bench verification) — baselines for extended dimensions captured there
- Related to br-8qdh0.7 (CI gate) — CI gate extended to include these dimensions

## Definition of done

- All 3 dimensions added to bench harness
- Baselines captured + committed to BUDGETS.md
- CI gate includes extended checks
- Negative test cases verify the checks actually fire
- Perf reports at `tests/artifacts/perf/extended_*` committed

title: Archive perf 13: read-path perf characterization (complement write-focused Epic 4)
description:
# Archive perf 13: Read-path perf characterization

## Why this bead exists

The archive perf epic is heavily write-focused (batch 100, coalescer, fsync). Read paths are arguably more frequent in practice:
- `fetch_inbox` — every agent session
- `resource://inbox/...` — operator + agent queries
- `resource://thread/...` — drill-downs
- `am robot inbox`, `am robot thread` — robot CLI
- Web UI `/mail/{project}/inbox/{agent}` — human oversight
- Search (`search_messages`) — all three: cold query, warm query, repeat query

No explicit benchmark coverage for read paths exists today in BUDGETS.md. Regressions (e.g., a schema migration that introduces a table scan, or a cache invalidation bug causing unnecessary reads) could land silently.

## Scope

### Benchmark additions

Add to `am bench` catalog:

| Benchmark | What it measures | Budget p95 |
|---|---|---|
| `inbox_fetch_small` | fetch_inbox with 10-row inbox | < 5ms |
| `inbox_fetch_large` | fetch_inbox with 10K-row inbox | < 50ms |
| `inbox_fetch_paginated` | fetch_inbox with limit=20 on 100K-row inbox | < 10ms |
| `thread_render_small` | thread with 10 messages | < 10ms |
| `thread_render_large` | thread with 1000 messages | < 100ms |
| `search_lexical_small` | 1K-doc corpus query | covered by br-o217s.4 fix baselines |
| `search_hybrid_small` | same corpus, hybrid routing (requires `hybrid` feature) | < 50ms |
| `resource_inbox` | HTTP GET resource://inbox/... | < 20ms |
| `robot_inbox` | `am robot inbox --format json` cold cache | < 30ms |
| `robot_inbox_cached` | same, warm cache | < 10ms |
| `web_ui_inbox` | HTTP GET /mail/{project}/inbox/{agent} | < 50ms |

### Concurrent read/write interference

New benchmark: `concurrent_inbox_read_during_writes`
- Baseline: N fetch_inbox calls against static DB
- Interference: same fetch_inbox with 100 concurrent send_message
- Assert: p95 increase < 10% under concurrent writes (WAL should make this cheap)

### Cache-coherency regression

The README describes "write-behind cache with dual-indexed ReadCache and deferred touch batching (30s flush)". If a write happens but the read cache doesn't invalidate, reads return stale data. Benchmark:
- Write a message; immediately fetch inbox; verify message present (correctness)
- Measure time from write to visibility (should be < 100ms; cache flush cadence determines this)

## Test plan

### Unit

- Each new bench runs cleanly, produces stable numbers across reruns
- Budgets not exceeded on reference hardware
- Negative test: inject artificial read latency → bench catches

### Integration

- Extended `am check perf-budgets` includes these benchmarks
- CI nightly: full read-path run with report

### Structured logging

```
perf.read_path.bench_start { scenario, dataset_size, cache_state: "cold"|"warm" }
perf.read_path.bench_complete { scenario, p50, p95, p99, throughput, cache_hits, cache_misses }
perf.read_path.concurrent_interference { scenario, baseline_p95, interfered_p95, increase_pct }
perf.read_path.cache_coherency { write_to_visibility_micros, stale_read: bool }
```

## Non-goals

- Not replacing existing write-focused benches (additive)
- Not optimizing read paths (characterization only; optimization is follow-up if regressions found)
- Not measuring all resource endpoints (focus on hot paths)

## Dependencies

- Depends on br-8qdh0.4 (write-path benches stable) — read benches use same harness
- Depends on br-8qdh0.8 (hardware docs) — read benches use same fingerprint
- Feeds br-8qdh0.7 (CI gate) — gate extended to read paths

## Definition of done

- All ≥10 new benchmarks added
- Baselines captured on reference hardware + in BUDGETS.md
- CI gate extended
- Cache-coherency test demonstrates bounded write-to-visibility latency
- Negative test verifies gate catches regressions

acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance criteria — test + logging rigor

### Pre-fix + post-fix bench comparison

- Baseline capture: pre-fix bench numbers committed to `tests/artifacts/perf/baseline_pre_fix_<date>.json`
- Post-fix capture: same bench against the fixed code, committed to `tests/artifacts/perf/baseline_post_fix_<date>.json`
- Diff artifact: `tests/artifacts/perf/fix_delta.json` showing per-op improvement
- All three artifacts committed in the same PR as the fix

### Mandatory tests (required to close bead)

1. **Batch 100 bench under budget** — p50 < 100ms, p95 < 250ms, p99 < 500ms
2. **Batch 10 bench** — p95 ≤ 50ms (intermediate size catches regressions that only emerge at scale)
3. **Batch 1000 bench** — verify scaling is sublinear (not perfectly linear would mean no amortization)
4. **Single-message path regression guard** — single-message p95 ≤ 25ms (no regression)
5. **Single-message + inline attachment p95 ≤ 25ms** (fix the prior 1.04x overrun as side-effect)
6. **30-agent stress (from README L262 10-test gauntlet)** — all tests still PASS
7. **WBQ saturation stress** — 2000 enqueues, 0 errors
8. **Coalescer batching ratio** — measure the observed batching under 100-write burst; document in test output

### Integration tests

- **Pre-commit guard still fires** — reservations enforcement unchanged
- **Git archive integrity** — run git fsck + verify every batch-written message has a canonical artifact file + both agent inbox/outbox copies
- **Doctor check** — `am doctor check` passes on post-batch-write DB

### Chaos tests

- Kill process mid-batch — recovery produces either complete batch or clean empty state (no partial batches committed)
- Fill disk mid-batch — batch fails cleanly, error returned to caller, no corruption

### Structured logging

All new log events use stable schema:
```
archive.batch_write.start { batch_size, agent, project_slug }
archive.batch_write.sqlite_phase { rows_inserted, duration_micros }
archive.batch_write.disk_phase { files_written, bytes_written, duration_micros }
archive.batch_write.git_phase { commits_created, duration_micros }
archive.batch_write.complete { total_duration_micros, batch_size }
```

Per-fix observability: if the fix introduces new primitives (e.g., batched-commit pathway), they emit dedicated spans with timing.

### Bench reproducibility

- Bench harness respects BUDGETS.md hardware documentation (see br-8qdh0.8)
- JSON output includes: hardware fingerprint, rust version, flags, timestamp, per-op p50/p95/p99/min/max + samples count

### Documentation

- If the fix changes public API / config, document in migration guide

title: Archive perf 7: CI perf-gate — bench on every PR; regression > 10% fails the build
description:
# Archive perf 7: CI perf regression gate

## Why this bead exists

Epic br-8qdh0 brings archive batch writes under budget. Without a CI gate, the same regression can reappear on any future PR touching storage/coalesce/archive. The reality-check identified that existing BUDGETS.md baselines are honest (dated) but there is no automated enforcement. Manual discipline has failed once (the 4x regression sat for 2+ months); we need it automated.

## Scope

Add a CI job that:
1. Runs `am bench --quick` (or targeted archive_write benches) against HEAD
2. Compares each operation's p95 against the BUDGETS.md budget
3. Fails the build if any operation exceeds budget * 1.1 (10% tolerance band for measurement noise)
4. Posts a PR comment with the measured numbers + delta vs. baseline
5. Allows a manual override label (`perf-regression-acknowledged`) for intentional changes (documented in PR body)

## Implementation options

### Option A: GitHub Actions workflow
```yaml
# .github/workflows/perf-gate.yml
name: Perf regression gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  bench:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest-with-consistent-hardware
    steps:
      - checkout
      - cargo bench ... > current.json
      - compare current.json vs benches/baseline.json
      - fail if any operation >10% over budget
```
- Pros: direct, PR visibility
- Cons: CI hardware noise; need consistent runner

### Option B: local pre-PR check
- Dev runs `am bench --gate` locally; CI just asserts no regression alert in the repo
- Pros: no CI noise
- Cons: easily forgotten

### Option C: nightly perf job + issue-on-regression
- Daily scheduled workflow + auto-creates a br issue when regression detected
- Pros: zero PR friction
- Cons: reactive not proactive

**Recommended: A + C combo.** A for PR-gate (fast feedback), C for long-horizon drift detection (slow creep that doesn't show up in single-PR deltas).

## Test plan

- Verify the gate fires on a deliberately regression-inducing PR (artificial sleep in coalesce.rs)
- Verify the gate does NOT fire on a no-op PR (typo fix)
- Verify the 10% tolerance band is honored (measurement noise doesn't flap the gate)
- Verify the manual override label works when applied
- Verify the comment posted to PR is readable and actionable

## Logging requirements

- CI output captures full bench report as an artifact (retained 30 days)
- PR comment includes: operation, current p95, budget, delta, verdict (pass/fail)
- Flaky runs (where the same code gives different numbers on different CI runs) are tagged and surface in a weekly report

## Hardware / reproducibility

- Pin the CI runner to `ubuntu-latest` with a specific instance class; document in the workflow file
- Optionally, use self-hosted runners on consistent hardware
- Document in `benches/BUDGETS.md`: "Baselines measured on <hardware-class>; CI gate compares against <hardware-class-note> with a 10% tolerance."

## Non-goals

- Not measuring every benchmark on every PR (slow); focus on the archive-write path which has a known regression history
- Not enforcing perf on unrelated crates (noise); scoped to mcp-agent-mail-storage + mcp-agent-mail-db

## Dependencies

- Depends on br-8qdh0.4 (bench verification) — baselines must be under budget before the gate can be meaningful
- Depends on br-8qdh0.6 (BUDGETS.md updated with new baselines) — gate compares against BUDGETS

## Definition of done

- Workflow file(s) committed and green on a no-op PR
- Deliberate regression test PR fails the gate as expected
- PR comment format is reviewed and approved
- Documentation in CONTRIBUTING.md or similar explains the gate for external contributors (even though we don't accept contributions — documentation is for our future self)
close_reason: CI perf regression gate landed in commit 323b934e per TopazSummit

# Archive perf 8: Hardware + reproducibility docs

## Why this bead exists

benches/BUDGETS.md records numbers but the reality-check noted it doesn't document the reference hardware. Without hardware context, numbers are meaningless to anyone re-running them on different machines. Also: environmental factors (kernel version, filesystem type, SSD vs HDD, swap pressure) strongly affect fsync and git-archive write speeds.

## Scope

Add a `## Hardware + Environment Baseline` section at the top of `benches/BUDGETS.md`:

```markdown
## Hardware + Environment Baseline

All baselines below measured on:

- **CPU**: <exact model, core count, base clock>
- **RAM**: <size, speed>
- **Storage**: <NVMe / SATA SSD / HDD; model; filesystem (ext4 / btrfs / xfs); mount options affecting fsync>
- **OS**: <distro + version + kernel version>
- **Rust toolchain**: <nightly date per rust-toolchain.toml>
- **Build profile**: release (opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1)
- **Workload isolation**: <taskset / cgroup / bare? whether CPU frequency scaling was disabled>
- **Runtime**: asupersync virtual-time baseline OR wall-clock? (determines stability of the numbers)

Re-running baselines: invoke `./scripts/bench_baseline.sh` which:
1. Captures the hardware + environment fingerprint
2. Runs the full bench suite with consistent settings
3. Emits JSON output comparable to BUDGETS.md
4. Writes a timestamped report to `tests/artifacts/bench/<date>/`
```

## Also deliverable: the `bench_baseline.sh` script

A repeatable harness that produces bit-exact comparable output whenever run on similar hardware.

## Test plan

- Run the script on reference machine; compare output to BUDGETS.md; verify numbers are in the same ballpark
- Run the script on a deliberately different machine (e.g., a laptop vs a server); verify the report captures the hardware delta and doesn't silently pretend numbers are comparable

## Logging requirements

- Each bench run produces a JSON summary with: hardware fingerprint, timestamp, rust version, flags, per-op numbers
- Runs across time can be diffed mechanically to detect drift
- A run that produces a missing fingerprint exits with an explicit error (don't allow unlabeled runs to pollute baselines)

## Non-goals

- Not attempting perfect portability (that's impossible for IO-bound benches)
- Not implementing CI cross-runner normalization

- The report JSON is parseable by the perf-gate in br-8qdh0.7

title: Archive perf 9: rollback plan for the perf fix if it regresses edge cases
description:
# Archive perf 9: Rollback plan

## Why this bead exists

The archive batch-write fix (br-8qdh0.3) may alter the commit coalescer, fsync strategy, archive file layout, or SQLite transaction semantics. Even with comprehensive testing (br-8qdh0.4-5), an edge case in production could surface: artifact durability regression, data corruption under power-loss, unexpected interaction with concurrent readers, etc.

We need a **tested rollback path** that reverts the fix in under 5 minutes without a full redeploy or data loss.

## Scope

### Rollback mechanism

The fix should be gated behind a feature flag (config env var, e.g., `ARCHIVE_WRITE_MODE=fast` for the fix, `ARCHIVE_WRITE_MODE=legacy` for pre-fix behavior, `ARCHIVE_WRITE_MODE=auto` for default).

- `fast` is the new default after the fix lands
- `legacy` preserves the pre-fix behavior (slower, but proven)
- `auto` is a transitional setting that tries fast, falls back to legacy on detected regression (e.g., disk-integrity check failure)

### Rollback procedure (runbook)

Add section to `docs/OPERATOR_RUNBOOK.md`:

```
## Emergency: roll back archive-write fix

Symptom: messages written but not visible on disk; doctor reports integrity errors.

Step 1: Set env ARCHIVE_WRITE_MODE=legacy, restart server.
Step 2: Run `am doctor check`, verify archive/DB parity.
Step 3: Run `am doctor repair --dry-run` to see if any rows need reconciliation.
Step 4: If repair is required, `am doctor repair --yes` will reconstitute from Git archive.
Step 5: File an incident bead referencing br-8qdh0 epic and describe what regressed.
```

### Feature-flag testing

- With ARCHIVE_WRITE_MODE=legacy on post-fix code, verify pre-fix perf profile (not budget-compliant, but behavior identical to pre-fix)
- With ARCHIVE_WRITE_MODE=fast, verify post-fix perf profile (budget-compliant)
- Mode-switch without restart: is this possible? If yes, test it. If no, document that rollback requires restart.

## Test plan

- Unit: each mode produces expected behavior
- Integration: simulate a regression scenario (e.g., mock a fsync failure), verify auto mode falls back correctly
- Chaos: pull the plug (kill -9) during batch write in each mode; verify no corruption, verify post-recovery state is consistent
- E2E: run the 10-test gauntlet with mode=fast (should pass under new budgets); with mode=legacy (should pass under old budgets)

## Logging requirements

- Mode-selection at startup emits INFO span: `archive.write_mode.selected { mode, source: "env"|"config"|"default" }`
- In `auto` mode, every fallback emits WARN span: `archive.write_mode.fallback { from: "fast", to: "legacy", reason }`
- Doctor check reports which mode the last write used (via a table metadata column or a run-log)

## Non-goals

- Not maintaining `legacy` mode forever — removal bead filed for 3 releases after the fix ships (giving users time to validate)
- Not designing multi-mode interop between versions

## Dependencies

- Depends on br-8qdh0.3 (fix implementation) — rollback is for that specific fix
- Depends on br-8qdh0.4 (bench verification) — need confirmed baselines for both modes

## Definition of done

- Feature flag implemented
- Both modes tested + benchmarked
- Runbook section committed
- Removal bead filed for T+3 releases

title: Add generation-keyed read snapshots for high-frequency mailbox views
description:
Goal: introduce short-lived generation-keyed read snapshots for hot mailbox views that many agents poll repeatedly: inbox metadata, reservations, project/agent rosters, and lightweight thread lists.

Rationale: massive swarms produce duplicate read work. A bounded snapshot keyed by project/product/agent plus DB generation can avoid recomputing identical views while preserving freshness. This complements, but is broader than, the robot-status-specific snapshot bead.

Scope: start with metadata-only views; full bodies and mutation responses stay uncached. Tie invalidation to message/reservation/agent write generations or conservative TTL.

Fallback/safe mode: stale or missing generation data disables the cache for that call.

Acceptance: cache key contract, invalidation tests, stale-generation fallback tests, memory cap tests, and a polling benchmark showing reduced DB query count without changing rendered JSON/toon output.
notes: Idea-wizard refinement pass: closure evidence should follow docs/VERIFICATION_COVERAGE_LEDGER.md. Prefer R0/R1 real-path evidence for transport, persistence, search, robot/operator, and load-lab claims. Performance acceptance should report p50/p95/p99 plus CPU/RSS/DB-query or queue-depth evidence where applicable. Test/repro workloads must use isolated STORAGE_ROOT and must not touch the operator mailbox. Stub-only tests can support design confidence but do not close user-facing or persistence/performance claims.

title: Epic: Git 2.51.0 concurrency hardening
description:
# Epic: Git 2.51.0 concurrency hardening

## Background / why this exists

System git `2.51.0` has a reproducible race in the cache_entry index walk.
Evidence (kernel log from the host running the agent swarm, 24h window):

    Apr 18 18:19–18:23   5 git segfaults in 4 minutes
    Apr 19 10:11–10:20   7 git segfaults in 9 minutes
    Apr 19 15:41–15:50   4 git segfaults in 9 minutes  (during an active session)
    TOTAL: 16 segfaults / 24h, all same instruction pointer.

Disassembly of the faulting instruction in `/usr/bin/git` (offset `1db240`):

    mov    0x0(%r13),%rax        ; rax = *r13 (pointer to index/cache table)
    mov    (%rax,%rbx,8),%r8     ; r8  = table[rbx] (entry pointer)
    mov    (%r8),%r12            ; r12 = *r8 (first object in chain)
    test   %r12,%r12             ; null check
    je     1db290                ; skip if null
    testb  $0x1,0x52(%r12)       ; <-- FAULT: reading ce_flags+0x52

The `0x52` offset + `0xe000` mask match `struct cache_entry` in git.
Interpretation: git is walking the staged index and dereferencing an entry
that was non-null at the check but pointed to unmapped memory at the deref.
Classic race: one git process rewrote/truncated a memory-mapped .git/index
(or pack file) while this one was reading it.

## Symptoms operators see

- Partial `.git/HEAD` / `.git/packed-refs` -> `fatal: bad object HEAD`
- Orphan `refs/stash` pointing to objects that were never fully written
  (lumera_ai_website reproduced this: ref exists, object does not)
- `ahead=-1 behind=-1` in `ru status` because the helper cannot resolve HEAD
- Fresh reclones corrupting again within minutes because parallel agents
  keep racing on the same `.git/index`

## Ruled out (for the record)

- SBH (Selective Ballast Handler) is NOT the culprit:
  /var/lib/sbh/activity.jsonl shows 0 matches for /dp/ or `.git`. It is only
  deleting /tmp/asupersync-* droppings and /data/tmp/cargo-target/*, and it
  honors file locks (SBH-2003 skipped: FileOpen).
- Disk pressure is NOT the culprit: / is 12% used.

## Key finding: where we shell out to /usr/bin/git in-process

The mcp-agent-mail server is LARGELY libgit2-based (git2 crate, vendored),
and the archive's `CommitCoalescer` already serializes writes per repo via
CAS. That archive surface is NOT the primary risk.

The primary risk is the six sites where we shell out to /usr/bin/git
against USER repos concurrently with the user's own `git commit`:

    | site                                              | op                                    |
    |---------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
    | storage/src/lib.rs:7341 (archive workdir)         | git read-tree HEAD (post-fail heal)   |
    | tools/src/resources.rs:3784                       | git log -1 --format=%ct -- <glob>     |
    | tools/src/resources.rs:3906                       | git ls-files -c -o ...                |
    | core/src/identity.rs:167                          | git config / git rev-parse            |
    | guard/src/lib.rs:1571/1610/1633                   | git diff --cached / rev-list / dtree  |
    | share/src/hosting.rs:236, share/src/detection.rs  | misc read-only                        |

These are the readers that can be in the middle of walking a cache_entry
table mmap'd from `.git/index` when a concurrent writer (the user's own
`git commit`) truncates+rewrites the same file.

## Why the obvious 'reserve .git/** with exclusive=true' fix is insufficient

Agent Mail file reservations are ADVISORY. They only gate agent-aware
writers through the pre-commit guard. The user's own `git commit` from an
IDE, CLI, or wrapper script has no knowledge of our reservation DB, so
wrapping agent git calls in a reservation doesn't stop the user's native
git from racing. We need OS-level coordination (fcntl flock) AND fewer
shell-outs in the first place.

## Plan (layers, execute 1->6)

1. Operator-facing: detect git 2.51.0 at install/runtime, warn loudly,
   add `AM_GIT_BINARY` config knob so operators can point to a safer git.
2. In-process per-repo mutex for OUR shell-outs. Eliminates self-races.
3. Cross-process OS flock on `<repo>/.git/am.git-serialize.lock` sentinel.
   Opt-in for external tools via a wrapper script. Does not close the
   unwrapped-git gap (layer 1 does).
4. Replace shell-outs with libgit2 where git2 already covers it. Removes
   race surfaces entirely.
5. SIGSEGV retry wrapper around remaining shell-outs as defense-in-depth.
6. `am doctor fix-orphan-refs` + periodic health sweep to clean up the
   damage that has already happened on repos that were hit before this
   landed.

## Success criteria

- Zero git segfaults in kernel log across 48h of a typical swarm session.
- No more `ahead=-1 behind=-1` from `ru status` after a session.
- No more `fatal: bad object HEAD` from agents picking up stale repos.
- `am doctor check` surfaces 2.51.0 as a known-bad version with remediation.
- Every in-process `Command::new('git')` in server+tools+storage either
  (a) goes through `run_git_locked`, or (b) has been migrated to git2.

## Non-goals

- Backporting a fix to upstream git. We coordinate around it; upstream
  will release 2.51.1 in their own time.
- Patching the guard's pre-commit `git diff --cached` call. The guard
  runs INSIDE the user's pre-commit process and cannot race against the
  commit that invoked it (same pid). We add SIGSEGV-retry as cheap
  insurance but we do NOT flock from inside the guard.
- Changing the mailbox archive commit path. The CommitCoalescer's per-repo
  CAS already serializes it; adding more locks there would only add cost.

## Workspace coverage map

    crates/mcp-agent-mail-core/src/git_lock.rs            <- NEW helper home
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-core/src/config.rs              <- AM_GIT_BINARY
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-core/src/identity.rs            <- migrate to git2
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-storage/src/lib.rs              <- drop read-tree shell-out
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-tools/src/resources.rs          <- migrate to git2
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-share/src/hosting.rs            <- audit + wrap or migrate
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-share/src/detection.rs          <- audit + wrap or migrate
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-guard/src/lib.rs                <- SIGSEGV retry only
    crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/doctor.rs               <- 2.51.0 detector, fix-orphan-refs
    install.sh                                            <- install-time warning
    README.md, RECOVERY_RUNBOOK.md                        <- known-bad version note
    scripts/git-with-amlock.sh                            <- NEW opt-in wrapper

## Ordering

See the dependency graph on this epic's children. Tracks A (docs/detection)
and B (locking helper) must land first; Track C (libgit2 migration) and
Track E (retry defense) sit on top of B; Track F (recovery) is independent;
Track G (release) is the fan-in.

## Known caveats

- The flock sentinel (`<repo>/.git/am.git-serialize.lock`) is opt-in.
  Unwrapped git processes (user's IDE) will not honor it. The only
  complete mitigation for those is layer 1 (downgrade/upgrade).
- libgit2's pathspec handling is slightly different from CLI git's
  `:(glob)` magic. Track C includes a parity test suite to catch
  regressions before we delete the shell-out fallbacks.
- `AM_GIT_BINARY` only helps child-process shell-outs. libgit2 calls
  don't care about the binary; they use the vendored library.

## Related memory / context

- See MEMORY.md: `feedback_never_touch_external_repos.md` — we MUST NOT
  run destructive git ops (reset --hard, clean -fd) against external
  repos, ever. Layer 6 (fix-orphan-refs) operates ONLY on refs, never on
  working tree contents, and only after the user explicitly invokes it.

title: Track A: Detection & Documentation for git 2.51.0
description:
# Track A: Detection & Documentation

**Goal:** make the 2.51.0 problem visible to operators BEFORE they hit it,
and give them a one-line way to point at a safer git binary.

## Why this track is P0

Every other mitigation in this epic is a partial fix (we can lock our own
processes, but the user's IDE-initiated `git commit` still races unless
they downgrade or upgrade). Detection + docs is the only mitigation that
addresses the unwrapped-git gap head-on. It must land first.

## Deliverables

1. `am doctor check` reports `git --version == 2.51.0` as a known-bad
   version with specific remediation text and a direct link to the
   RECOVERY_RUNBOOK entry.
2. `install.sh` emits the same warning at install time (non-blocking;
   we don't refuse to install, we just tell the user).
3. README gets a `Known-bad git versions` subsection under Troubleshooting.
4. RECOVERY_RUNBOOK.md gets the kernel-log fingerprint, disassembly, and
   downgrade/upgrade instructions so ops can diagnose the same symptom
   again without re-investigating.
5. New config env var `AM_GIT_BINARY` (default `git`): all in-process
   shell-outs resolve their git binary through this so operators can
   point the server at `/usr/local/git-2.50.1/bin/git` without touching
   PATH.

## Scope boundaries

- This track does NOT change any shell-out call sites yet. It only
  introduces the config var + the detector. Track B rewrites call sites
  to honor `AM_GIT_BINARY`.
- This track does NOT run any destructive git command. It reads `git
  --version`, that's it.

## Success signals

- `am doctor check` on a box with git 2.51.0 prints a RED section with
  text matching `GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD` so grep can spot it.
- A fresh install on a box with git 2.51.0 prints the same warning
  before the first binary runs.

title: A1: Research — confirm git 2.51.0 bug scope and upstream status
description:
# A1: Research bug scope and upstream status

## Why

Before we ship warnings with specific version ranges, we need to know
whether the bug is 2.51.0-only, whether a 2.51.1 has shipped, and
whether it touches only the index mmap path or also packed-refs /
loose-ref paths.

## Tasks

- [ ] Pull the git 2.51.0 release tag from kernel.org mirror and inspect
      the cache_entry (index) code path around offset 0x52 (ce_flags).
- [ ] Search git-scm.com and the git mailing list for concurrency fixes
      that landed between 2.51.0 and HEAD.
- [ ] Confirm whether 2.51.1 exists and what it fixes.
- [ ] Check whether the same bug shape exists in the 2.52.x series.
- [ ] Identify the canonical Debian/Ubuntu/macOS/Homebrew package versions
      that happen to ship 2.51.0.
- [ ] Write a 1-page finding to 'docs/GIT_251_FINDINGS.md' (new file)
      with exact commit SHAs, issue references, and recommended
      version ranges.

## Output

- `docs/GIT_251_FINDINGS.md` with a clear 'use >= X and != 2.51.0'
  recommendation. This feeds A2/A3/A4.

## Non-goals

- Do NOT patch git. Do NOT submit a fix upstream. This is read-only
  research.

title: A2: 'am doctor check' detects git 2.51.0 and prints remediation
description:
# A2: am doctor check detects git 2.51.0

## Why

Operators reach for `am doctor` when a project starts misbehaving.
Making the 2.51.0 check a first-class doctor finding means the first
thing an operator sees is 'here's your problem and here's how to fix
it', not 'something is vaguely wrong'.

## Implementation

- Add a new check in `crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/doctor.rs`
  named `check_git_version_known_bad`.
- Logic:
    - Resolve the git binary via `AM_GIT_BINARY` (see A5); default 'git'.
    - Run `<git> --version` with a 5-second timeout. If spawn fails,
      report 'git binary not found' (existing pattern) and move on.
    - Parse the semver. If it equals 2.51.0 exactly, emit a FAIL level
      finding with:
        - code:    GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD
        - summary: short one-line
        - detail:  multi-line including kernel log fingerprint signature
                   (instruction pointer, offset) so operators can
                   grep-verify.
        - fix:     'set AM_GIT_BINARY=/path/to/git-2.50 OR upgrade system
                   git to 2.51.1+'.
    - If it is in a version range that A1 flags as broken, emit the
      same FAIL. Otherwise WARN on any 2.51.x until A1 finishes.
- Wire the finding into the JSON schema used by `am doctor check
  --format json` so programmatic callers (NTM, CI) can assert on it.

## Success signals

- `am doctor check` on a 2.51.0 box prints a RED section containing
  `GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD`.
- `am doctor check --format json | jq '.findings[] | select(.code ==
  \"GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD\")'` returns a non-empty match on the same box.

## Tests

- Unit test in `doctor.rs` that feeds a fake version string and asserts
  the finding shape.
- Integration test in `tests/e2e/test_doctor_git_version.sh` that mocks
  git with a shim script and verifies the exit code + stdout substring.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## REVISION v2: AM_GIT_BINARY awareness + exit codes + logging

### Additions to the check logic

- The doctor check resolves the git binary via `resolved_git_binary()`
  (A5), NOT raw PATH. Ops who set AM_GIT_BINARY expect the check to
  operate on THAT binary.
- The check also inspects the default PATH git separately. Both are
  reported so operators can see 'you set AM_GIT_BINARY=<safe>, but
  your default git is still 2.51.0 — guard hooks and external tools
  will still use the broken one.' This is the failure mode we saw in
  the original report.
- Output schema (JSON) — one finding per resolution:
    {
      "code": "GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD",
      "severity": "fail",
      "resolution": "AM_GIT_BINARY" | "path",
      "path": "/usr/bin/git",
      "version": "2.51.0",
      "remediation": "...",
      "kernel_fingerprint": "ip 0x1db250, err 4"
    }
- New exit code mapping:
    0 — all checks pass
    1 — non-fatal warnings (existing semantics)
    2 — fatal checks (existing semantics)
    3 — GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD found. Distinct so CI can specifically
        gate on it without coupling to other check failures.

### Structured logging (target: mcp_agent_mail::doctor)

- INFO on each check start/end with duration_ms.
- FAIL finding emits WARN with code, version, path, resolution.

### Unit tests (crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/src/doctor.rs)

- test_check_git_version_known_bad_2_51_0_exact
- test_check_git_version_ok_on_2_50_x
- test_check_git_version_ok_on_2_52_x
- test_check_git_version_parse_failure_handled
- test_check_reports_both_env_and_default_binary_when_divergent
- test_check_emits_json_shape_matches_schema

### Integration test (crates/mcp-agent-mail-cli/tests/doctor_git_251.rs)

- Builds two PATH shims:
    shim_251: prints 'git version 2.51.0'
    shim_ok:  prints 'git version 2.50.2'
- Matrix:
    PATH=<shim_ok>, AM_GIT_BINARY=unset -> exit 0, no finding.
    PATH=<shim_251>, AM_GIT_BINARY=unset -> exit 3, finding present.
    PATH=<shim_251>, AM_GIT_BINARY=<shim_ok> -> exit 3 with BOTH
         findings (default is broken even if env is fine).
    PATH=<shim_ok>,  AM_GIT_BINARY=<shim_251> -> exit 3, env finding.

### E2E test (tests/e2e/test_doctor_git_version.sh)

- Invokes `am doctor check --format json` with the shim matrix above.
- jq-validates the JSON schema (pulled from docs/schemas/doctor.json).
- Prints ISO-8601 timestamps at each step; saves artifacts under
  tests/artifacts/doctor_git_251/ for CI archival.

### Non-goals (unchanged)

Still just detection + reporting. No auto-repair, no auto-download.

title: A3: install.sh warns about git 2.51.0 at install time
description:
# A3: installer warning for git 2.51.0

## Why

Most users install via the curl pipe. If their box has 2.51.0 we should
say so on the very first command before they've even used the server.

## Implementation

- In `install.sh`, after the preflight environment checks, add a
  `check_git_version_known_bad` shell function that:
    - Runs `git --version 2>/dev/null | awk '{print \$3}'`.
    - If equal to '2.51.0', prints a prominent YELLOW warning to stderr
      (using the existing `_say warn` helper):
        'Detected git 2.51.0 which has a concurrency bug that corrupts
         .git/index under load. Consider downgrading to 2.50.x or
         upgrading to 2.51.1+. See RECOVERY_RUNBOOK.md for details, or
         set AM_GIT_BINARY to a safer binary.'
    - Does NOT abort the install. This is a warning, not a gate.
- Covered by `tests/installer/test_install_warn_git_251.sh` using a
  PATH-shim git.

## Non-goals

- Do not auto-install a different git. That's operator policy.
- Do not refuse the install.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## REVISION v2: Installer warning details + tests

- The installer uses the same resolution logic as A5/A2 where possible:
  if `AM_GIT_BINARY` is set in env at install time, warn about THAT
  binary; otherwise warn about default PATH git. Document both.
- The warning goes to stderr (not stdout) so that any consumer that
  pipes install.sh output to a log file captures it, and so that
  `install.sh | bash` doesn't surface the warning as install stdout.
- Text template (exact wording, include markers so ops can grep):
    [AM_INSTALL_WARN GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD]
    Detected git 2.51.0 which has a concurrency bug that corrupts
    .git/index under multi-agent load. Symptoms: segfaults, bad HEAD,
    orphan stashes. Remediation:
      1. Set AM_GIT_BINARY=/path/to/git-2.50.x in your shell profile
      2. Upgrade to git >= 2.51.1 once released
      3. Run 'am doctor fix-orphan-refs --apply' on damaged repos
    Details: RECOVERY_RUNBOOK.md#git-2-51-0-index-race

### Tests

- tests/installer/test_install_warn_git_251.sh:
  - PATH-shimmed tempdir, shim_251 reports 2.51.0.
  - Runs install.sh --dry-run (should not touch filesystem) and captures
    stderr.
  - asserts stderr matches /AM_INSTALL_WARN GIT_2_51_0_KNOWN_BAD/.
  - Second run with shim_ok asserts stderr does NOT match the warning.
- Each script step echoes 'INSTALL_TEST_STEP <n>' with timestamp for
  post-hoc review, and artifacts go to tests/artifacts/installer/.

### Non-goals (unchanged)

Never aborts install. Never modifies PATH.

2. Expand RECOVERY_RUNBOOK.md with a new section 'Git 2.51.0 index

        1. Run `am doctor check` to confirm.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## REVISION v2: Docs scope + link hygiene + verification

### Added content requirements

- README 'Troubleshooting' section gains:
    ### Known-bad git versions

    mcp-agent-mail interacts with git in several places. Some git
    versions have concurrency bugs that cause the server and agents
    to race against each other, corrupting .git/index under load.

    | Version  | Status              | Mitigation                      |
    |----------|---------------------|---------------------------------|
    | 2.51.0   | KNOWN BAD (segfault)| AM_GIT_BINARY, upgrade to >=2.51.1, or downgrade to 2.50.x |

    Run `am doctor check` to see if your system git is affected.

- RECOVERY_RUNBOOK.md gains a full section with EXACT reproducible
  diagnostic commands:

    ### Diagnosing git 2.51.0 index race

    Check kernel log for the fingerprint:

        journalctl -k --since '24 hours ago' | awk '/segfault/ && /git\\[/'

    A stream of `ip 0x1db250 error 4` lines is the signature.

    Disassemble to confirm (optional):

        objdump -d $(which git) --start-address=0x1db240 \\
          --stop-address=0x1db260 | head -40

    The faulting line should be `testb \$0x1,0x52(%r12)` — that's
    `cache_entry::ce_flags` being dereferenced after the entry pointer
    was invalidated by a concurrent writer.

    Symptoms in your repos:
    - `fatal: bad object HEAD` after a session
    - orphan `refs/stash` (ref exists, object missing)
    - `ahead=-1 behind=-1` in tooling
    - fresh reclones corrupting again within minutes

    Remediation (in order):
    1. `am doctor check`
    2. Set `AM_GIT_BINARY=<safe git>` or upgrade/downgrade system git.
    3. `am doctor fix-orphan-refs --project <path> --dry-run`
    4. Review planned actions. When satisfied, `--apply`.

### Link hygiene

- README -> RECOVERY_RUNBOOK anchor is tested in docs CI.
- CHANGELOG entry (G3) links here for users doing upgrade diligence.

### Verification

- docs/check_doc_links.sh walks all internal .md links and fails on
  dangling anchors. Runs in G1 quality gate.
- Manual check: render README on github.com and click through to
  ensure anchor renders correctly (no underscores -> hyphens issues).

### Non-goals

- No marketing copy; this is a technical runbook.
